thread.title: Tech Stocks Usually Fall as Apple Drops. Things Could Be Better Now. - Barron's

title: Tech Stocks Usually Fall as Apple Drops. Things Could Be Better Now. - Barron's
text:
Tech Never Shines When Apple Stock Slumps. Things Could Be Better This Time. By Jan. 9, 2019 6:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Kevin Frayer/Getty Images Text size
Trouble for Apple usually brings a downturn for the tech sector in general. The latest slide in Apple stock (ticker: AAPL)—a 35% decline since October—is no exception, but the damage could be more contained than in the past.
Technology stocks in the S&P 500 have fallen 17% since October, underperforming the broader index by 5.3 percentage points. “The S&P 500 Technology sector has never outperformed the S&P 500 when AAPL has plummeted more than 30%,” Ohsung Kwon, strategist at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, wrote in a research note on Tuesday, suggesting a comeback isn’t likely unless Apple shares recover.
Still, he says, the picture this time might be brighter than history suggests. Apple stock has gone through three major selloffs in the current economic cycle: the 44.4% dive from September 2012 through April 2013, the 32.1% drop from February 2015 to May 2016, and the 35% plunge we are seeing now, triggered by signs of weaker iPhone sales .
Each time, the tech sector went underwater along with Apple, but to different extents. Tech stocks in the S&P 500 underperformed the broader index by 18 percentage points during Apple’s 2012 pullback, but only suffered an 8 percentage-point lag in 2015, according to Kwon. Newsletter Sign-up
Apple’s representation in the S&P 500 could be one explanation. The iPhone maker’s market capitalization made up 24.1% of the total for the whole tech sector when the stock peaked in 2015, Bloomberg figures show, much less than the 29.6% at its 2012 peak. The ratio was still lower, at 21.2%, this past October. Less representation means the stock would have less impact on the whole sector’s performance.
Why investors were selling Apple also matters. While 2012’s selloff was caused by issues specific to Apple—worries about a supposed lack of innovation—the 2015 decline was triggered by broader issues such as an economic slowdown in China, Apple’s fastest-growing market at the time.
Kwon believes the current selloff is a combination of both, estimating that about 60% of Apple’s reduction in its revenue forecast for the December quarter was due to weakness in China. That implies the rest of the cut resulted from problems at the company itself.
“The smartphone market is much more mature now than it was back in 2012-13 when it was a market with tremendous growth opportunities for not just AAPL but also for other tech companies,” he writes. “Therefore, slowing phone sales pose less risk to the sector today vs. back then.”
Kwon believes the tech sector has already priced in the risk of a slowdown in emerging markets, suggesting that the potential rewards are attractive relative to the risks, especially if a favorable trade deal between the U.S. and China can be made.
Another piece of good news: If Apple stock reaches a bottom in the near future , the tech sector will likely rally as well, Kwon says. Tech stocks in the S&P 500 outperformed the index by 7.2 percentage points over the 12 months that followed Apple’s 2013 trough, and by 21.9 percentage points after its 2016 low point. The outperformance stands even after excluding Apple’s contribution.
The sector is currently trading at 15.2 times forward earnings, writes Kwon, only slightly higher than the overall S&P 500.
